newsitem.title: CANADA: Alberta, Ontario to lead Canada economy, bank says.
newsitem.headline: Alberta, Ontario to lead Canada economy, bank says.

text.p: Canada's two most fiscally conservative provinces, Alberta and Ontario, will lead the pack in economic growth during the next two years, said a report by a large Canadian bank.

Alberta's economy will grow by 4.4 percent during each of the next two years, while Ontario will enjoy growth of 3.8 percent this year and 4.0 percent in 1998, the Bank of Montreal predicted in its regional economic outlook.
Low interest rates, easing of fiscal policy and improving consumer confidence are the main reasons for the expected boom, said Tim O'Neill, the bank's chief economist.
"Alberta is benefiting from booming production in the oil and gas fields, strong cash flow in the agricultural sector, and economic diversification," O'Neill said.
An increase in consumer confidence is shifting the Alberta economy into high gear, O'Neill added.
Ontario's growth will be spurred by manufacturers of transportation equipment, chemicals and machinery, and also from the financial services sector, the bank said.
Ontario's gross domestic product (GDP) rose 1.75 percent last year. Alberta's projected growth is more than double its annual GDP during the past two years.
Canada's three remaining western provinces were expected to grow in a range of 2.5 to 3.5 percent.
Saskatchewan will grow the least at 2.5 percent this year and 2.75 percent in 1998.
A decline in agricultural production from last year's above average harvest would dampen the overall pace of economic expansion in the prairie province, O'Neill said.

Some economic softening would occur despite good international demand prospects for Saskatchewan's key agricultural and mining products and strengthening conditions in the manufacturing sector, O'Neill said.
The bank said it would release its regional economic outlooks for Quebec and the Maritime provinces on Thursday.
